nodes.name: Multiple zeta values
nodes.statement: Multiple zeta values are real numbers, defined for a collection $n_1,\dots,n_r$ of positive integers, with $n_r > 1$, by the nested sum \[ \zeta(n_1,\dots,n_r)=\sum_{0<k_1<k_2<\dots <k_r}\frac{1}{k^{n_1}_1k^{n_2}_2\dots k^{n_r}_r}. \]
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: MZV $\zeta(n_1,\dots,n_r)$ as the nested sum over $0<k_1<\dots<k_r$ of $1/k_1^{n_1}\cdots k_r^{n_r}$.

nodes.name: Weight and depth of multiple zeta values
nodes.statement: The \textit{weight} is the quantity $n_1+\dots+n_r$ and the \textit{depth} is the number $r$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Ihara-Kaneko-Zagier conjecture
nodes.statement: A conjecture, due to Ihara, Kaneko and Zagier~\cite{IKZ}, states that all such relations are obtained from the \textit{extended double-shuffle relations}, which, roughly speaking, arise from rewriting the product of two multiple zeta values in two different ways as $\mathbb Q$-linear combinations of other multiple zeta values.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: All Q-linear relations among MZVs follow from the extended double-shuffle relations.
conclusions: all such relations are obtained from the \textit{extended double-shuffle relations}

nodes.name: Iterated integral
nodes.statement: Let $\omega_1,\dots,\omega_r$ be a collection of smooth one-forms on a complex manifold $M$, and let $\gamma: [0,1] \rightarrow M$ be a piecewise smooth path. Write $f_i(t)\mathrm{d} t$ for the pull back of $\omega_i$ along $\gamma$. We define \begin{equation} \int_{\gamma}\omega_1\dots\omega_r:=\int_{0<t_1<\dots<t_r<1}f_1(t_1)\mathrm{d} t_1\dots f_r(t_r)\mathrm{d} t_r. \end{equation} and call this integral an \emph{iterated integral}. More generally, every $\mathbb C$-linear combination of iterated integrals as above will also be called an iterated integral. If $r=0$, we set $\int_{\gamma}=1$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries
nodes.statement_short: Iterated integral of one-forms along a path: integral of pulled-back forms over the simplex $0<t_1<\dots<t_r<1$; linear combinations included.

nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: Odd Jacobi theta function
nodes.statement: We consider a version of the odd Jacobi theta function $\theta_{\tau}$, defined for $\xi \in \mathbb C$ by \begin{equation} \theta_{\tau}(\xi):=\sum_{n \in \mathbb Z}(-1)^nq^{\frac{1}{2}(n+\frac{1}{2})^2}e^{(n+\frac{1}{2})2\pi i\xi}, \quad q=e^{2\pi i\tau}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Kronecker series
nodes.statement: The \textit{Kronecker series} $F_{\tau}: \mathbb C \times \mathbb C \rightarrow \mathbb C$~\cite{W,Z} is the meromorphic function defined by the formula \begin{equation} F_{\tau}(\xi,\alpha)=\frac{\theta_{\tau}'(0)\theta_{\tau}(\xi+\alpha)}{\theta_{\tau}(\xi)\theta_{\tau}(\alpha)}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries
nodes.statement_short: $F_\tau(\xi,\alpha)=\theta'(0)\theta(\xi+\alpha)/(\theta(\xi)\theta(\alpha))$.

nodes.statement: F_{\tau}(\xi,\alpha)=\frac{\theta_{\tau}'(0)\theta_{\tau}(\xi+\alpha)}{\theta_{\tau}(\xi)\theta_{\tau}(\alpha)}.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: Quasi-periodicity of the Kronecker series
nodes.statement: The Kronecker series is quasi-periodic with respect to lattice translations in both variables \begin{align} F_{\tau}(\xi+1,\alpha)=F_{\tau}(\xi,\alpha), \quad F_{\tau}(\xi+\tau,w)=e^{-2\pi i\frac{\mathrm{Im}(\xi)}{\mathrm{Im}(\tau)}\alpha}F_{\tau}(\xi,\alpha), \\ F_{\tau}(\xi,\alpha+1)=F_{\tau}(\xi,\alpha), \quad F_{\tau}(\xi,\alpha+\tau)=e^{-2\pi i\frac{\mathrm{Im}(\alpha)}{\mathrm{Im}(\tau)}\xi}F_{\tau}(\xi,\alpha). \end{align}
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries
conclusions: The Kronecker series is quasi-periodic with respect to lattice translations in both variables

nodes.name: Properties of $\Omega_\tau$: periodicity, symmetry, Fay identity, modularity
nodes.statement: The one-form $\Omega_{\tau}(\xi,\alpha)$ satisfies the following properties: \begin{enumerate} \item It is doubly periodic in $\xi$: \begin{align} \Omega_{\tau}(\xi+1,\alpha)=\Omega_{\tau}(\xi,\alpha), \quad \Omega_{\tau}(\xi+\tau,\alpha)=\Omega_{\tau}(\xi,\alpha). \end{align} Thus it descends to a formal differential one-form on $E^{\times}_{\tau}$. \item It is symmetric in its arguments, i.e. \begin{equation} \Omega_{\tau}(-\xi,-\alpha)=\Omega_{\tau}(\xi,\alpha). \end{equation} \item It satisfies the Fay identity: \begin{align} \Omega_{\tau}(\xi_1,\alpha_1) \land \Omega_{\tau}(\xi_2,\alpha_2)&=\Omega_{\tau}(\xi_1-\xi_2,\alpha_1) \land \Omega_{\tau}(\xi,\alpha_1+\alpha_2) \notag \\ &+\Omega_{\tau}(\xi_2-\xi_1,\alpha_2) \land \Omega_{\tau}(\xi,\alpha_1+\alpha_2). \end{align} \item We have the modular transformation formula \begin{equation} \Omega_{\frac{a\tau+b}{c\tau+d}}((c\tau+d)^{-1}\xi,(c\tau+d)^{-1}\alpha)=(c\tau+d)\Omega_{\tau}(\xi,\alpha) \end{equation} for $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix} \in \mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Properties of $\omega^{(k)}$: modular weight, parity, Fay identity
nodes.statement: The form $\omega^{(k)}$ has modular weight $k+1$, i.e. \begin{equation} \omega^{(k)}_{\vert \gamma}=(c\tau+d)^{k+1}\omega^{(k)} \end{equation} where the action of $\gamma \in \mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$ on $\omega^{(k)}$ is defined as in~\eqref{eqn:Omegamod}. Moreover, $\omega^{(k)}=f^{(k)}(\xi)\mathrm{d}\xi$ is doubly periodic and antisymmetric/symmetric depending on the weight \begin{equation} f^{(k)}(-\xi)=(-1)^kf^{(k)}(\xi), \end{equation} and we have the Fay identity \begin{align} f^{(m)}(\xi_1)f^{(n)}(\xi_2)&=-(-1)^nf^{(m+n)}(\xi_1-\xi_2) \notag\\ &+\sum_{r=0}^{n}\binom{m+r-1}{m-1}f^{(n-r)}(\xi_2-\xi_1)f^{(m+r)}(\xi_1) \notag\\ &+\sum_{r=0}^{m}\binom{n+r-1}{n-1}f^{(m-r)}(\xi_1-\xi_2)f^{(n+r)}(\xi_2). \end{align} \qed

nodes.name: A-elliptic multiple zeta value
nodes.statement: We define the A-elliptic multiple zeta value $I^A(n_1,\dots,n_r;\tau)$\footnote{In \cite{BMMS}, this is denoted by $\omega(n_1,...,n_r)$} to be the coefficient of $\mathrm{ad}^{n_1}(x)(y)\dots\mathrm{ad}^{n_r}(x)(y)$ in the regularized generating series \begin{equation} \lim_{t \to 0}(-2\pi it)^{\mathrm{ad}(x)(y)}\exp\bigg[\int_{\alpha_t^{1-t}}\mathrm{ad}(x)\Omega_{\tau}(\xi,\mathrm{ad}(x)(y))\bigg](-2\pi it)^{-\mathrm{ad}(x)(y)}, \end{equation} where $\alpha_t^{1-t}$ denotes the restriction of the path $\alpha$ to the interval $[t,1-t]$, and for a differential one-form $\omega$, we write \begin{equation} \exp\bigg[\int \omega\bigg]=1+\sum_{k \geq 1}\int \underbrace{\omega\dots\omega}_{\textrm{k-times}}. \end{equation} The regularization of the integral is performed as in~\cite{Del}, Proposition 15.45 (with the order of integration reversed), with respect to the tangent vector $-\frac{\partial}{\partial z}=(-2\pi i)^{-1}\frac{\partial}{\partial \xi}$ at $0$ at the starting point of the path of integration (where $z=e^{2\pi i\xi}$), and with respect to the tangent vector $\frac{\partial}{\partial z}=(2\pi i)^{-1}\frac{\partial}{\partial \xi}$ at $0$ at the endpoint of the path of integration.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.2
nodes.statement: Recall that $A(\tau)$ is defined as \begin{equation} A(\tau)=X(z)^{-1}X(z+1), \end{equation} where $X(z)$ is the unique holomorphic function defined on $\{z \in \mathbb C \, | \, z=u+vi, \ u \mbox{ or } v \in (0,1)\} \subset \mathbb C$, which solves the equation \begin{equation} \mathrm{d} X(z)=-\mathrm{ad}(x)\Omega_{\tau}(\xi,\mathrm{ad}(x))(y) \cdot X(z), \end{equation} and satisfies $X(z) \sim (-2\pi iz)^{-\mathrm{ad}(x)(y)}$, as $z \to 0$, where we choose the principal branch of the logarithm so that $\log(\pm i)=\pm \frac{\pi i}{2}$. Using Picard iteration, and standard properties of iterated integrals (cf.~Section~2.1), we see that $A(\tau)$ equals \begin{align} \bigg(\lim_{t \to 0}(-2\pi it)^{\mathrm{ad}(x)(y)}\exp\bigg[\int_{\alpha_t^{1-t}}(-\mathrm{ad}(x)\Omega_{\tau}(\xi,\mathrm{ad}(x)(y)))\bigg]e^{\pi i\mathrm{ad}(x)(y)}(-2\pi it)^{-\mathrm{ad}(x)(y)}\bigg)^{op}, \end{align} where the superscript $op$ denotes the opposite multiplication on the algebra $\mathbb C \langle\langle x,y\rangle\rangle$, defined by $(f \cdot g)^{op}=g \cdot f$. Now multiplying by $e^{-\pi i\mathrm{ad}(x)(y)}$, the result follows.

nodes.statement_short: Solve the KZB-type equation for $X(z)$ by Picard iteration and express $A(\tau)$ as the opposite of the regularised series.

nodes.name: B-elliptic multiple zeta values
nodes.statement: In~\cite{E}, one also finds a notion of B-elliptic multiple zeta value, which we denote here by $I^B(n_1,\dots,n_r;\tau)$, defined as iterated integrals along the other homology cycle $\beta$ of an elliptic curve. Similar to A-elliptic multiple zeta values, B-elliptic multiple zeta values can be obtained as coefficients of Enriquez's B-associator~\cite{E2}. The modular transformation formula (cf.~\cite{E}, eq.~(26)) \begin{equation} I^B(n_1,\dots,n_r;\tau)=\tau^{-(n_1+\dots+n_r)+r}I^A(n_1,\dots,n_r;-\tau^{-1}) \end{equation} establishes a close connection between A-elliptic and B-elliptic multiple zeta values. A more detailed treatment of B-elliptic multiple zeta values will be given elsewhere.

nodes.statement_short: B-elliptic MZVs integrate along $\beta$ and are related to A-elliptic ones by a modular transformation.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.6
nodes.statement: We use induction on the set of multi-indices of a fixed length $r$, ordered lexicographically. For $\underline{n}=(0,\dots,0) \in \mathbb N^r$, it is clear that \begin{equation} I^A(0,\dots,0;\tau)=T^{\mathrm{Reg}}(\alpha)_{y^r}. \end{equation} Now let $\underline{n}=(n_1,\dots,n_r)$ be a multi-index of length $r$ and assume the proposition for all multi-indices $\underline{n'}$ such that $\underline{n'} \prec \underline{n}$ in the lexicographical ordering. Now by \eqref{eqn:transl}, we have \begin{equation} I^A(\underline{n};\tau)=(-1)^{n_1+\dots+n_r}\left(T^{\mathrm{Reg}}(\alpha)_w-\sum_{\underline{n'} \prec \underline{n}} c_{\underline{n'}}I^A(\underline{n'};\tau) \right), \end{equation} where $w=yx^{n_1}\dots yx^{n_r}$. The terms on the right hand side of the last equation can be expressed as coefficients of $T^{\mathrm{Reg}}(\alpha)$, by the induction hypothesis, and this ends the proof.

nodes.name: Representation-theoretic interpretation of $W_N$
nodes.statement: Moreover, $W_N$ has the following representation-theoretic interpretation. A polynomial $P \in W_N$ can be viewed as a representation $\mathcal{P}$ of the symmetric group $S_3$: the two-dimensional $\mathbb Q$-vector space $\mathcal{P} \subset \mathbb Q[X,Y]$ spanned by $P(X,Y),P(Y,-X-Y)$ is acted upon by $S_3$ by \begin{equation} (12) \mapsto (P(X,Y) \mapsto P(-Y,-X)), \quad (123) \mapsto (P(X,Y) \mapsto P(Y,-X-Y)). \end{equation} Note that $(12)$ acts with trace $0$ and that $(123)$ acts with trace $-1$. Thus, it follows from the elementary representation theory of the symmetric group $S_3$ (cf.~e.g.~\cite{Ser}, Chap.~2) that $\mathcal{P}$ is necessarily isomorphic to the unique irreducible, two-dimensional $S_3$-representation $\mathcal W$. Also, since $P$ has degree $N$, and $\mathbb Q[X,Y]$ is naturally isomorphic to $\bigoplus_{N \geq 0}\mathrm{Sym}^N \mathcal W$, the representation $\mathcal{P}$ can be viewed as a sub-representation of $\mathrm{Sym}^N \mathcal W$. Conversely, given a sub-representation $\mathcal{P}$ of $\mathrm{Sym}^N \mathcal W$ isomorphic to $\mathcal W$, one verifies directly that there exists a unique (up to a non-zero scalar) element $P \in \mathcal{P}$ such that $P \in W_N$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.2
nodes.statement: We first assume that $b\leq a/2$. In that case, the right hand side is equal to \begin{equation} \binom{a-b+1}{a-2b+1}{}_{3}F_{2}\left[\begin{smallmatrix}a-b+1,&-b/2+1/2,&-b/2\\\\&a/2-b+1,&a/2-b+3/2\end{smallmatrix};1\right], \end{equation} where ${}_{3}F_{2}$ is a hypergeometric function (cf.~\cite{B}, Chapter~II). If $b$ is even, we can apply Saalsch"utz's Theorem about ${}_3F_2$ (cf.~\cite{B}, Section~2.2), namely \begin{equation} {}_3F_2\left[\begin{smallmatrix}a,&b,&-n\\\\&c,&a+b+c+1-n\end{smallmatrix};1\right]=\frac{(c-a)_n(c-b)_n}{(c)_n(c-a-b)_n}, \end{equation} where $(m)_k:=m(m+1)\dots(m+k-1)$ denotes the Pochhammer symbol. Hence, \eqref{eqn:app1} is equal to \begin{equation} \binom{a-b+1}{a-2b+1}\frac{(-a/2)_{b/2}(a/2-b/2+1/2)_{b/2}}{(a/2-b+1)_{b/2}(-a/2+b/2-1/2)_{b/2}}=\binom{a}{b}. \end{equation} In the case where $b$ is odd, we can apply Saalsch"utz's Theorem after interchanging $-b/2$ and $-b/2+1/2$ in the argument of ${}_3F_2$ in \eqref{eqn:app1} above, and get the result. If $b>a/2$, then the same argument as above works, with $b$ replaced by $a-b$ throughout.

nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the sum as a ${}_3F_2$ at $1$ and evaluate by Saalschutz's theorem, by parity of $b$; the case $b>a/2$ by symmetry.

nodes.name: Case $i\ge 2j+1$: both sides vanish.
nodes.statement: For $i \geq 2j+1$, both sides of \eqref{eqn:binom2} are evidently equal to zero.

nodes.statement_short: Case $i\ge 2j+1$: both sides vanish.

nodes.name: Case $i=0$: both sides equal 1.
nodes.statement: If $i=0$, then, since $l_{0,k}=\delta_{0,k}$, both sides of \eqref{eqn:binom2} are equal to $1$.

nodes.name: Remaining case $0<i<2j+1$.
nodes.statement: It remains to prove \eqref{eqn:binom2} for $i,j$ such that $0<i<2j+1 \leq n$, i.e. \begin{align} \binom{2j+1}{i}-\delta_{2j+1,i}&=\sum_{k=1}^n\binom{k}{i-k}\binom{2j-k}{k-1}\frac{2j+1}{k} \notag\\ &=\sum_{k=1}^i\binom{k}{i-k}\binom{2j-k}{k-1}\frac{2j+1}{k}. \end{align} Note that $\binom{k}{i-k}$ vanishes for $k > i$.
